claim: Long-term synaptic plasticity can be expressed both pre- and postsynaptically.
source: Although it is well known that long-term synaptic plasticity can be expressed both pre- and postsynaptically, the functional consequences of this arrangement have remained elusive.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the abstract.

claim: Spike-timing-dependent plasticity with both pre- and postsynaptic expression develops receptive fields with reduced variability compared to postsynaptic plasticity alone.
source: We show that spike-timing-dependent plasticity with both pre- and postsynaptic expression develops receptive fields with reduced variability and improved discriminability compared to postsynaptic plasticity alone.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract, supported by the modeling and simulation results presented in the manuscript.

claim: Spike-timing-dependent plasticity with both pre- and postsynaptic expression develops receptive fields with improved discriminability compared to postsynaptic plasticity alone.
source: We show that spike-timing-dependent plasticity with both pre- and postsynaptic expression develops receptive fields with reduced variability and improved discriminability compared to postsynaptic plasticity alone.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract, supported by the modeling and simulation results presented in the manuscript.

claim: Long-term modifications in receptive field statistics from the unified plasticity model match recent sensory perception experiments.
source: These long-term modifications in receptive field statistics match recent sensory perception experiments.
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison with experimental data from Froemke et al. (2013) as described in the manuscript.

claim: Learning with unified pre- and postsynaptic plasticity leaves a hidden postsynaptic memory trace that enables fast relearning of previously stored information.
source: Moreover, learning with this form of plasticity leaves a hidden postsynaptic memory trace that enables fast relearning of previously stored information, providing a cellular substrate for memory savings.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract, supported by the memory savings simulations presented in the manuscript.

claim: The hidden postsynaptic memory trace provides a cellular substrate for memory savings.
source: Moreover, learning with this form of plasticity leaves a hidden postsynaptic memory trace that enables fast relearning of previously stored information, providing a cellular substrate for memory savings.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the modeling results presented in the manuscript.

claim: Presynaptic plasticity has essential roles that are missed when only postsynaptic expression of long-term plasticity is considered.
source: Our results reveal essential roles for presynaptic plasticity that are missed when only postsynaptic expression of long-term plasticity is considered, and suggest an experience-dependent distribution of pre- and postsynaptic strength changes.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the modeling results comparing unified plasticity to postsynaptic-only plasticity.

claim: There is an experience-dependent distribution of pre- and postsynaptic strength changes.
source: Our results reveal essential roles for presynaptic plasticity that are missed when only postsynaptic expression of long-term plasticity is considered, and suggest an experience-dependent distribution of pre- and postsynaptic strength changes.
evidence: This is suggested based on the modeling results and their interpretation.

claim: The Tsodyks-Markram model with facilitation was used to model short-term synaptic plasticity.
source: To model short-term synaptic plasticity, we used the Tsodyks-Markram model with facilitation (Markram et al., 1998).
evidence: This is a methodological statement citing the model used.

claim: Between spikes, r recovers to 1 with a depression time constant D.
source: Between spikes r recovers to 1 with a depression time constant D.
evidence: This describes the mathematical formulation of the model.

claim: The presynaptic factor p increases an amount P[1 − p] after every presynaptic spike.
source: The second equation models the dynamics of the presynaptic factor p which increases an amount P[1 − p] after every presynaptic spike, decaying back to baseline presynaptic factor P with a facilitation time constant F.
evidence: This describes the mathematical formulation of the model.

claim: The presynaptic factor p decays back to baseline presynaptic factor P with a facilitation time constant F.
source: The second equation models the dynamics of the presynaptic factor p which increases an amount P[1 − p] after every presynaptic spike, decaying back to baseline presynaptic factor P with a facilitation time constant F.
evidence: This describes the mathematical formulation of the model.

claim: Typical values for pyramidal-onto-pyramidal synapses are D = 200 ms and F = 50 ms.
source: We used typical values for pyramidal-onto-pyramidal synapses (Costa et al., 2013), D = 200 ms and F = 50 ms, while P is modified by long-term plasticity as below.
evidence: This is a methodological statement citing parameter values used in the model.

claim: The average number of vesicles released per spike is r(t)p(t), which can be interpreted as the presynaptic strength.
source: The average number of vesicles released per spike is r(t)p(t), which can be interpreted as the presynaptic strength.
evidence: This is a definition provided in the model description.

claim: In layer-5 pyramidal to pyramidal cell synapses, timing-dependent LTD is presynaptically expressed.
source: In layer-5 pyramidal to pyramidal cell synapses, timing-dependent LTD is presynaptically expressed.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about the biological system.

claim: Timing-dependent LTD is mediated by the coincidence between a postsynaptic signal (eCB release) and a presynaptic signal (presynaptic NMDA receptor activation).
source: It is mediated by the coincidence between a postsynaptic signal (eCB release) and a presynaptic signal (presynaptic NMDA receptor activation) (Sjöström et al., 2003, 2004; Bender and Feldman, 2006; Yang and Calakos, 2013).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claim: LTP is driven by postsynaptic coincidence detection of the combined binding of glutamate and postsynaptic depolarization.
source: LTP is driven by postsynaptic coincidence detection of the combined binding of glutamate and postsynaptic depolarization (Bender and Feldman, 2006; Sjöström et al., 2007; Shouval et al., 2010), promoting an increase in the number and/or properties of postsynaptic AMPA receptors (Malinow and Malenka, 2002).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: LTP promotes an increase in the number and/or properties of postsynaptic AMPA receptors.
source: LTP is driven by postsynaptic coincidence detection of the combined binding of glutamate and postsynaptic depolarization (Bender and Feldman, 2006; Sjöström et al., 2007; Shouval et al., 2010), promoting an increase in the number and/or properties of postsynaptic AMPA receptors (Malinow and Malenka, 2002).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: Timing-dependent LTP has a presynaptic component mediated by postsynaptic diffusion of NO.
source: However, timing-dependent LTP also has a presynaptic component, mediated by postsynaptic diffusion of NO (Hardingham and Fox, 2006; Sjöström et al., 2007; Hardingham et al., 2013; Yang and Calakos, 2013).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claim: The phenomenological triplet model of long-term modification has three synaptic traces: two postsynaptic (y+ and y−) and one presynaptic (x+).
source: Our phenomenological triplet model of long-term modification of pre- and postsynaptic components has three synaptic traces, two postsynaptic (y+ and y−) and one presynaptic (x+), which increase upon a post- or presynaptic spike, respectively (see Appendix 1 for a more detailed comparison with the triplet model (Pfister and Gerstner, 2006)).
evidence: This is a description of the model developed in the manuscript.

claim: The synaptic traces increase upon a post- or presynaptic spike.
source: Our phenomenological triplet model of long-term modification of pre- and postsynaptic components has three synaptic traces, two postsynaptic (y+ and y−) and one presynaptic (x+), which increase upon a post- or presynaptic spike, respectively (see Appendix 1 for a more detailed comparison with the triplet model (Pfister and Gerstner, 2006)).
evidence: This is a description of the model developed in the manuscript.

claim: The traces are obtained by filtering the spike trains with a first-order low-pass filter.
source: The traces are obtained by filtering the spike trains with a first-order low-pass filter.
evidence: This is a methodological description of the model.

claim: The long-term modification in the weight is achieved by modifying the postsynaptic factor q and the presynaptic factor P.
source: The long-term modification in the weight is achieved by modifying the postsynaptic factor q and the presynaptic factor P.
evidence: This is a description of the model developed in the manuscript.

claim: LTP only takes place when the postsynaptic spike follows both a presynaptic spike and a preceding postsynaptic spike.
source: This ensures that LTP only takes place when the postsynaptic spike follows both a presynaptic spike and a preceding postsynaptic spike (Pfister and Gerstner, 2006).
evidence: This is an explanation of the model behavior, supported by a citation.

claim: Low pairing frequencies do not lead to LTP because y− will have decayed.
source: As a result, low pairing frequencies do not lead to LTP, as y− will have decayed, consistent with data (Sjöström et al., 2001).
evidence: This is an explanation of the model behavior, consistent with cited experimental data.

claim: For plasticity in P to occur, the presynaptic spikes readout the postsynaptic traces.
source: For plasticity in P to occur, the presynaptic spikes X readout the postsynaptic traces (presynaptic coincidence detection), y−y+ for presynaptic LTD and x+y+ for presynaptic LTP.
evidence: This is a description of the model developed in the manuscript.

claim: Presynaptic LTD has a triplet form containing two postsynaptic traces and the raw presynaptic spike train.
source: While presynaptic LTD has a triplet form, it contains two postsynaptic traces and the raw presynaptic spike train.
evidence: This is a description of the model developed in the manuscript.

claim: Presynaptic LTD does not vanish at low frequencies.
source: Therefore it does not vanish at low frequencies.
evidence: This is an explanation of the model behavior.

claim: For a synapse that has not been stimulated recently, the synaptic strength simplifies to w = Pq.
source: For a synapse that has not been stimulated recently this simplifies to w = Pq.
evidence: This is a mathematical simplification of the model.

claim: P is hard-bounded between 0 and 1 as it is a probability.
source: Being a probability we hard-bounded P = [0, 1].
evidence: This is a constraint applied in the model based on the biological interpretation of P.

claim: The postsynaptic factor q has a lower bound of 0 and an upper bound of 2.
source: The postsynaptic factor q had a lower bound of 0, and an upper bound of 2.
evidence: This is a constraint applied in the model.

claim: Postsynaptic homosynaptic LTD was not apparent on the timescale of the experiment in the data used to fit the model.
source: In the data used to fit the model (see below), postsynaptic homosynaptic LTD was not apparent on the timescale of the experiment.
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data used for model fitting.

claim: Slow homeostatic scaling of the postsynaptic factor was included for network simulations.
source: Because it seems unrealistic that the postsynaptic factor q never decreases, slow homeostasic scaling of the postsynaptic factor was included for network simulations (Turrigiano et al., 1998).
evidence: This is a methodological choice made for the simulations, supported by a citation.

claim: Homeostatic scaling prevents weakly active synapses from potentiating the postsynaptic factor q.
source: This prevents weakly active synapses from potentiating the postsynaptic factor q.
evidence: This is an explanation of the functional role of homeostatic scaling in the model.

claim: The speed of homeostatic scaling should not lead to noticeable homeostasis on the timescale of the experiments.
source: The only condition on the speed α for it to be consistent with the data, is that it should not lead to noticable homeostasis on the timescale of the experiments.
evidence: This is a constraint applied to ensure consistency with experimental data.

claim: α = 0.075 was used for computational efficiency, which is still orders of magnitude faster than what has been observed in homeostasis experiments.
source: For computational efficiency we used α = 0.075, which is still orders of magnitude faster than what has been observed in homeostasis experiments.
evidence: This is a methodological statement about parameter choice.

claim: The exact form of slow normalization (α → 0) does not affect the qualitative behavior of the model.
source: The exact form of slow normalization (α → 0) does not affect the qualitative behavior of the model.
evidence: This is a statement about the robustness of the model to parameter choices.

claim: The timescale of the slow normalization determines how long the memory savings effects are present.
source: Note that the timescale of the slow normalization determines how long the memory savings effects are present.
evidence: This is an explanation of how a model parameter affects a specific outcome.

claim: The free parameters of the long-term plasticity model were fitted to frequency- and timing-dependent slice STDP data of layer-5 pyramidal cells.
source: We fitted the free parameters of the long-term plasticity model θ = {d−, τy−, d+, τy+, c+, τx+} to the frequency- and timing-dependent slice STDP data of layer-5 pyramidal cells (Sjöström et al., 2001).
evidence: This is a methodological statement about model fitting to experimental data.

claim: The model was fitted directly to modifications in P and q rather than to changes in the weight w.
source: Rather than fitting to changes in the weight w, we fitted directly to modifications in P and q (see Equations 21, 22 for our estimators of P and q).
evidence: This is a methodological statement about the fitting procedure.

claim: The fitting was done by minimizing the mean squared error between the data and the experiments for both P and q.
source: This was done by minimizing the mean squared error between the data and the experiments for both P and q (as shown in Figure 1)
evidence: This is a methodological statement about the fitting procedure, with reference to a figure.

claim: For induction protocols at high frequencies (≥10 Hz), pre- and postsynaptic spike trains consisted of five spikes that were paired 15 times at 0.1 Hz.
source: For induction protocols at high frequencies (≥10 Hz), pre- and postsynaptic spike trains consisted of five spikes that were paired 15 times at 0.1 Hz.
evidence: This is a methodological statement about the simulation protocol.

claim: Low-frequency pairings (0.1 Hz) were done with a single pre- and postsynaptic spike.
source: Low-frequency pairings (0.1 Hz) were done with a single pre- and postsynaptic spike (as in Sjöström et al., 2001).
evidence: This is a methodological statement about the simulation protocol, consistent with cited experimental procedures.

claim: Before plasticity induction, P and q were set to 0.5 and 1, respectively.
source: Before plasticity induction, P and q were set to 0.5 and 1, respectively.
evidence: This is a methodological statement about initial conditions in the simulations.

claim: For the interaction of STP and STDP simulations, a standard passive neuron model with a membrane time constant of 25 ms was used.
source: For the interaction of STP and STDP simulations (Figure 1F,G), we used a standard passive neuron model with a membrane time constant of 25 ms.
evidence: This is a methodological statement about the neuron model used in specific simulations.

claim: The model without further fitting captured pharmacological blockade of the plasticity traces.
source: Without further fitting this model also captured pharmacological blockade of the plasticity traces.
evidence: This is a statement about the model's ability to reproduce additional experimental results without additional parameter fitting.

claim: The experimental effects of pharmacological blockade were simulated by setting the relevant parameter or variable to 0.
source: In the model, we simulated the experimental effects of pharmacological blockade by setting the relevant parameter or variable to 0.
evidence: This is a methodological statement about how pharmacological manipulations were modeled.

claim: eCB signaling is involved in STDP in layer-5 pyramidal cell pairs.
source: Specifically, we simulated the effects of blocking two different retrograde messenger systems shown to be involved in STDP in layer-5 pyramidal cell pairs, eCB signaling (Sjöström et al., 2003) and NO signaling (Sjöström et al., 2007).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: NO signaling is involved in STDP in layer-5 pyramidal cell pairs.
source: Specifically, we simulated the effects of blocking two different retrograde messenger systems shown to be involved in STDP in layer-5 pyramidal cell pairs, eCB signaling (Sjöström et al., 2003) and NO signaling (Sjöström et al., 2007).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Blocking eCB receptors prevents presynaptic LTD.
source: Blocking eCB receptors prevents presynaptic LTD (Sjöström et al., 2003).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: Setting d− = 0 in the model disables presynaptic LTD.
source: By setting d− = 0 presynaptic LTD was disabled.
evidence: This is a methodological statement about how eCB blockade was simulated.

claim: Blocking eCB receptors reveals presynaptic LTP and enhances short-term depression.
source: This reveals presynaptic LTP and enhances short-term depression (Figure 1—figure supplement 3), consistent with experimental evidence (Sjöström et al., 2007), as the drugs used are likely to block presynaptic eCB receptors.
evidence: This is a result from the model simulations that is consistent with cited experimental evidence.

claim: Blocking NO decreases LTP but does not affect short-term synaptic dynamics.
source: In contrast, blocking NO decreases LTP but does not affect short-term synaptic dynamics (Sjöström et al., 2007) (Figure 1—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by a citation and shown in a figure.

claim: NO blockade was simulated by setting y+ = 0, so that both presynaptic components were absent.
source: We simulated this by setting y+ = 0, so that both presynaptic components were absent.
evidence: This is a methodological statement about how NO blockade was simulated.

claim: The release of neurotransmitter was assumed to follow a standard binomial model.
source: The release of neurotransmitter was assumed to follow a standard binomial model (Del Castillo and Katz, 1954)
evidence: This is a methodological statement about the model used, supported by a citation.

claim: The number of release sites N is believed to change only after a few hours.
source: The number of release sites N is believed to change only after a few hours (Bolshakov et al., 1997; Saez and Friedlander, 2009).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: The slice synaptic plasticity experiments lasted only up to 1.5 hr.
source: As the slice synaptic plasticity experiments analysed here lasted only up to 1.5 hr (Sjöström et al., 2001) and we were interested in the relative changes we assumed constant N = 5.5 in our analysis below, as estimated in Markram et al. (1997) using data from the same connection type we used to fit our model.
evidence: This is a statement about the experimental data used, supported by a citation.

claim: N was assumed constant at 5.5 in the analysis.
source: As the slice synaptic plasticity experiments analysed here lasted only up to 1.5 hr (Sjöström et al., 2001) and we were interested in the relative changes we assumed constant N = 5.5 in our analysis below, as estimated in Markram et al. (1997) using data from the same connection type we used to fit our model.
evidence: This is a methodological statement about an assumption made in the analysis, based on cited estimates.

claim: Equations 21, 22 were used to estimate P and q from in vitro plasticity data.
source: Equations 21, 22 were used to estimate P and q from in vitro plasticity data (see above), respectively (dataset deposited at Dryad data repository at http://dx.doi.org/10.5061/dryad.p286g [Costa et al., 2015]).
evidence: This is a methodological statement about data analysis, with reference to a data repository.

claim: There are minor differences in the mean weights compared to previously published values due to full reanalysis of the data.
source: Note that because the data had to be reanalized in full there are minor differences in the mean weights previously published (Sjöström et al., 2001).
evidence: This is a note about differences between the current analysis and previously published results.

claim: The P and q extraction method was verified by analysing short-term plasticity experiments with pharmacological manipulation of presynaptic release or of postsynaptic gain.
source: We verified our P and q extraction method by analysing short-term plasticity experiments with pharmacological manipulation of presynaptic release or of postsynaptic gain (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A, Sjöström et al., 2003), and experiments with pharmacological blockade of pre- or postsynaptic long-term plasticity (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B, Sjöström et al., 2007) (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A,B).
evidence: This is a methodological statement about validation of the extraction method using experimental data.

claim: Long-term changes in P but not in q were inversely correlated with changes in paired-pulse ratio.
source: In addition, long-term changes in P but not in q were inversely correlated with changes in paired-pulse ratio, as expected (Figure 1—figure supplement 2C,D).
evidence: This is a result from the data analysis that matches expectations.

claim: The binomial-distribution-based approach for extracting P and q is supported by experimental evidence.
source: Taken together, these results lend experimental support to our binomial-distribution-based approach for extracting P and q to tune changes in the pre- and postsynaptic modifications of our unified STDP model (Figure 1D,E).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the validation analyses.

claim: The effective P and q were extracted from in vivo data obtained by Froemke et al. (2013).
source: We extracted the effective P and q from the in vivo data obtained by Froemke et al. (2013).
evidence: This is a methodological statement about analysis of published experimental data.

claim: A binomial model was used to obtain estimators for the variability measure v = q (1 − P) and the mean μ = PqN.
source: Again using a binomial model, we obtained estimators for their variability measure given by v = q (1 − P) and the mean by μ = PqN.
evidence: This is a methodological statement about the analysis approach.

claim: The initial P was set to 0.5 to ease comparison with simulations.
source: To ease comparison with our simulations we set the initial P to the same initial condition used in our simulations P = 0.5 (Costa et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a methodological statement about parameter choice for analysis.

claim: After pairing, both pre- and postsynaptic factors P and q were allowed to change, while N was fixed.
source: For the after pairing data we allowed both pre- and postsynaptic factors P and q to change, while N was fixed to the values extracted before pairing (Bolshakov et al., 1997).
evidence: This is a methodological statement about the analysis approach, with a citation supporting the assumption about N.

claim: The experimentally obtained q was scaled such that before plasticity it was 1 to ease comparison with simulations.
source: To ease comparison with the postsynaptic factor in the simulations we scaled the experimentally obtained q such that before plasticity it was 1.
evidence: This is a methodological statement about data normalization.

claim: Models where both P and q change had lower variability estimation error compared to models where only one factor changes.
source: We compared models where we allowed both P and q to change or only one of them, the lower variability estimation error was obtained by the one where both factors change (Figure 2—figure supplement 3E).
evidence: This is a result from model comparison analysis.

claim: After unified STDP, the first response has a higher amplitude and the second one a much lower amplitude due to synaptic depression.
source: After unified STDP the first response has a higher amplitude and the second one a much lower amplitude due to synaptic depression.
evidence: This is a result from the model simulations.

claim: Combined with background noise, the SNR can drop when the second or further responses are included.
source: Combined with the background noise, the SNR can drop when the second or further responses are included.
evidence: This is an explanation of a phenomenon observed in the model.

claim: The SNR of the summed response will always be larger than when only postsynaptic modifications are made.
source: However, the SNR of the summed response will always be larger than when only postsynaptic modifications are made (see Figure 2—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is a result from the model analysis shown in a figure.

claim: The SNR advantage of unified plasticity holds for any frequency.
source: This holds for any frequency, Figure 2—figure supplement 2C and carries over to an information theoretic analysis of the response, Figure 2—figure supplement 2D.
evidence: This is a result from the model analysis shown in figures.

claim: ROC analysis was used to compute the false alarm and detection probability of the first postsynaptic response.
source: Next, we used ROC analysis to compute the false alarm and detection probability of the first postsynaptic response
evidence: This is a methodological statement about the analysis approach.

claim: The overall discriminability was assessed using pdiscrimination, which is the area under the ROC curve (AUC).
source: To assess the overall discriminability, we used pdiscrimination, which is the area under the ROC curve (AUC).
evidence: This is a methodological statement about the discriminability measure used.

claim: The AUC was computed by integrating over the ROC curve using the trapezoid method.
source: The AUC was computed by integrating over the ROC curve using the trapezoid method (see Figure 2D).
evidence: This is a methodological statement about the computation method.

claim: For receptive field development simulations, a feedforward network with 100 presynaptic neurons and a single integrate-and-fire postsynaptic neuron was used.
source: For the receptive field development simulations, we used a feedforward network with 100 presynaptic neurons j with Poisson statistics and a single integrate-and-fire postsynaptic neuron.
evidence: This is a methodological statement about the network architecture used in simulations.

claim: The postsynaptic neuron was modelled as an adaptive exponential integrate-and-fire neuron model.
source: The postsynaptic neuron was modelled as an adaptive exponential integrate-and-fire neuron model (Brette and Gerstner, 2005).
evidence: This is a methodological statement about the neuron model used, supported by a citation.

claim: Model parameters were as reported in Brette and Gerstner (2005) and Badel et al. (2008).
source: Model parameters were as reported in Brette and Gerstner (2005); Badel et al. (2008) and synapses were modelled as input currents.
evidence: This is a methodological statement about parameter sources.

claim: The maximum and minimum rates were set to ρmax = 50 Hz and ρmin = 3 Hz.
source: ρmax and ρmin are the maximum and minimum rates, and were set to ρmax = 50 Hz and ρmin = 3 Hz.
evidence: This is a methodological statement about parameter values.

claim: d−, d+ and c+ were scaled by a factor 0.15 to yield a smoother receptive field development.
source: We scaled d−, d+ and c+ by a factor 0.15 to yield a smoother receptive field development.
evidence: This is a methodological statement about parameter scaling.

claim: q was bounded between 0 nA and 20 nA so that the synaptic input is appropriately scaled for the neuron model used.
source: q was bounded between 0 nA and 20 nA, so that the synaptic input is appropriately scaled for the neuron model used.
evidence: This is a methodological statement about parameter bounds.

claim: The network was simulated for 100 s to achieve convergence.
source: The network was simulated for 100 s to achieve convergence.
evidence: This is a methodological statement about simulation duration.

claim: For the memory savings experiment, two receptive field positions were interleaved.
source: For the memory savings experiment, we interleaved two receptive field positions.
evidence: This is a methodological statement about the experimental protocol.

claim: Results for receptive development and memory savings were averaged over 10 runs.
source: Results for receptive development and memory savings were averaged over 10 runs.
evidence: This is a methodological statement about data averaging.

claim: The response of the postsynaptic neuron was assessed by presenting each stimulus alone with long-term synaptic plasticity inactive.
source: The response of the postsynaptic neuron (Figure 3C) was assessed by presenting each stimulus alone with long-term synaptic plasticity inactive.
evidence: This is a methodological statement about response assessment.

claim: Receptive field simulations were implemented in simulator Brian 1.41.
source: Receptive field simulations were implemented in simulator Brian 1.41 (Goodman and Brette, 2008).
evidence: This is a methodological statement about the simulation software used.

claim: Code for running and plotting the savings experiment is available online at http://modeldb.yale.edu/184487.
source: Code for running and plotting the savings experiment is available online (http://modeldb.yale.edu/184487).
evidence: This is a statement about code availability.

claim: Statistical comparisons were made with Student's t-test for equal means if data was normally distributed.
source: Statistical comparisons were made with Student's t-test for equal means, if data was normally distributed as assessed using Kolmogorov–Smirnov test, Mann–Whitney U non-parametric test was used otherwise.
evidence: This is a methodological statement about statistical testing.

claim: Mann–Whitney U non-parametric test was used for non-normally distributed data.
source: Statistical comparisons were made with Student's t-test for equal means, if data was normally distributed as assessed using Kolmogorov–Smirnov test, Mann–Whitney U non-parametric test was used otherwise.
evidence: This is a methodological statement about statistical testing.

claim: For multiple comparisons, ANOVA was applied for normally distributed data.
source: For multiple comparisons we applied ANOVA or Kruskal–Wallis test for normally or non-normally distributed data, respectively.
evidence: This is a methodological statement about statistical testing.

claim: For multiple comparisons, Kruskal–Wallis test was applied for non-normally distributed data.
source: For multiple comparisons we applied ANOVA or Kruskal–Wallis test for normally or non-normally distributed data, respectively.
evidence: This is a methodological statement about statistical testing.

claim: For correlation analysis, the Spearman's coefficient was used together with one-tailed Student's t-test.
source: For correlation analysis the Spearman's coefficient was used together with one-tailed Student's t-test.
evidence: This is a methodological statement about statistical testing.
